items.title: Navibulgar adds handymax pair to growing China orderbook
items.original_title: Navibulgar adds handymax pair to growing China orderbook
items.summary: Bulgarian dry bulk owner Navibulgar has returned to China’s Yangzijiang Shipbuilding for another pair of handymax bulk carriers, expanding its newbuilding programme to 13 vessels. The Varna-based company has signed up for two 47,000 dwt bulkers at Jiangsu New Yangzi Shipbuilding, with both scheduled for delivery in 2030. Financial terms have not been disclosed. Navibulgar’s own fleet register confirms the vessels, identifying them as Vihren , due in February 2030, and Botev , earmarked for April of the same year. The pair also matches two 47,000 dwt bulk carriers included in Yangzijiang’s latest stock exchange update, which showed the orders already on its books at the end of October. The latest additions extend Navibulgar’s long-running fleet renewal programme at the Chinese shipbuilding group. The owner has three 45,000 dwt handymaxes scheduled for delivery in 2027, followed by eight 71,000 dwt bulkers due between 2028 and 2029. The company has been steadily investing in larger and more efficient geared bulkers while maintaining a sizeable presence in the handysize and handymax markets. Its existing fleet includes several 47,000 dwt vessels built between 2019 and 2020, including Buzludja, Midjur, Malyovitsa and Milin Kamak .

items.title: EDT Offshore kicks off fleet renewal with subsea newbuild
items.original_title: EDT Offshore kicks off fleet renewal with subsea newbuild
items.summary: Cyprus-based EDT Offshore has ordered a subsea construction vessel at China’s ZPMC, with an option for a second unit, kicking off a newbuilding programme aimed at expanding its offshore capabilities. The Limassol-headquartered owner has signed a contract with the Shanghai-based shipbuilder for a Skipsteknisk-designed energy subsea construction vessel (ESCV), with delivery scheduled for early 2029. The ST-245 design methanol-ready newbuilding will feature an integrated electric propulsion system, battery storage, DC switchboards, azimuth thrusters and dynamic positioning technology. “This order is a major commitment to EDT’s future,” said managing director Darios Melas. EDT has also brought in Schulte Marine Concept to supervise construction at the Chinese yard. The family-controlled company operates a fleet of offshore support and multipurpose vessels, with activities spanning subsea construction support, offshore energy operations, towage and salvage. Last year, EDT teamed up with Singapore’s Synergy Marine Group to establish EDT Synergy Shipmanagement, a Cyprus-based venture targeting the offshore vessel management market. Norwegian naval architect Skipsteknisk has seen growing demand for its ST-245 platform, which has also been selected by Rem Offshore and Sea1 Offshore for their subsea and offshore energy support newbuilding programmes. For ZPMC, the contract adds to its offshore vessel portfolio, which includes service operation vessels, heavylift ships and other specialised construction tonnage.

items.title: UK port congestion, empty-container restrictions add upward pressure to freight rates
items.original_title: UK port congestion, empty-container restrictions add upward pressure to freight rates
items.summary: Congestion across the UK container logistics network is tightening effective vessel and equipment capacity, adding upward pressure to freight prices as carriers contend with import backlogs, schedule disruption and restrictions on empty-container returns. Maersk said in a Nov. 24 customer advisory that sustained high import volumes, network congestion, adverse weather and recent rail disruption had placed pressure on UK and Ireland port and landside operations. 24, Maersk said in a separate customer advisory, while Felixstowe Quay and Tilbury Quay remained closed to empties pending planned evacuation operations. The restrictions risk extending truck turn times and repositioning distances while reducing the speed at which equipment can be returned to circulation. With blank sailings further narrowing available vessel space, UK congestion is expected to remain a source of upward pressure on freight prices until terminals clear backlogs and empty equipment begins circulating more normally. Platts Container Rate 1 (PCR1) – North Asia to North Europe – and Platts Container Rate 11 (PCR11) – North Asia to the UK – were last assessed Nov. 24 at $3,400 per FEU. Platts Container Rate 3 (PCR3) – North Asia to the Mediterranean – was assessed at $5,400 per FEU.

items.title: GPCA ’26: GCC retains cost edge but faces structural shifts – ICIS
items.original_title: GPCA ’26: GCC retains cost edge but faces structural shifts – ICIS
items.summary: Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) petrochemical producers retain a significant cost advantage but need to rethink strategies as oversupply, weaker demand, and shifting trade flows reshape the industry, according to ICIS consultants. The Middle East remains among the lowest-cost regions for ethylene production because of access to advantaged ethane and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), with most regional capacity in the first half of the global cost curve, according to an ICIS presentation at the Gulf Petrochemicals and Chemicals Association (GPCA) Annual Forum in Dubai on 23 November. But cost competitiveness alone may no longer guarantee market share as China becomes increasingly self-sufficient, sustainability changes the polymer demand mix, and recent disruptions demonstrate the risks associated with export-dependent business models. Demand for key polymers is projected to increase by around 50% between 2025 and 2050, according to ICIS Supply & Demand Database projections. By 2050 those shares could rise to 31%, 30% and 33%, respectively, under an ICIS scenario. Global net crude oil demand could decline by around 340 million tonnes between 2025 and 2040 as biofuels, renewables, and natural gas liquids take a larger share of overall oil demand, ICIS vice president, oil products & feedstocks Stefano Zehnder said.

items.title: The Commodities Feed: Copper and gold rebound while oil extends gains
items.original_title: The Commodities Feed: Copper and gold rebound while oil extends gains
items.summary: Energy – Middle East risks lift oil prices ICE Brent extended gains for a fourth consecutive session on Friday, trading above $97/bbl and heading for its first weekly gain this month. Prices remain supported by attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping in the Middle East. The latest disruption involved Saudi Arabia’s 400k b/d Jazan refinery, following earlier attacks on the Ras Tanura export hub and Red Sea ports, adding uncertainty around the recovery in regional crude exports. Singapore stocks, meanwhile, increased by 949k barrels to 40.9m barrels, driven by higher light distillate and residual fuel stocks, while middle distillates edged lower. Metals – Copper rebounds as risk appetite improves Copper extended its recovery on Friday, with LME prices climbing back above $12,600/t after falling below $11,500/t earlier in the week. The Yangshan premium has eased from last week’s record levels of $500/t but remains elevated at around $320/t, while the spread between Chinese spot prices and international benchmarks continues to point to a premium for metal in China. Focus will remain on Chinese demand and inventories, as well as the potential movement of US-held copper back into the global market. Gold also moved higher on Friday, recovering further from the 15-month low reached earlier this week as stronger equity markets and a softer US dollar offered some support.

items.title: Pakistan’s coal imports surge 51% as LNG supplies collapse
items.original_title: Pakistan’s coal imports surge 51% as LNG supplies collapse
items.summary: The fallout from the Middle East conflict is generating significant new employment opportunities for mid-sized bulkers, with Pakistan’s dramatic switch from gas to coal providing one of the clearest examples yet of how disruption to one shipping sector is driving demand in another.< Research from BRS Shipbrokers shows Pakistan’s seaborne coal imports surged 51.2% year-on-year to 11.52m tonnes in the first 10 months of 2026, while LNG imports slumped 55.1% to 2.82m tonnes. Pakistan’s overwhelming reliance on Qatari LNG has left it particularly exposed to disruption at Qatar’s Ras Laffan export facilities and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The extent of the country’s fuel switching is particularly striking. Electricity generation from imported coal soared 237% year-on-year in October, while LNG-fired generation contracted by 61%. South Africa has accounted for around 93% of Pakistan’s additional coal imports this year, with shipments climbing from 4.73m tonnes to 8.36m tonnes. Supramax and ultramax bulkers have been the principal beneficiaries, accounting for around 94% of voyages between South Africa and Pakistan, with their combined voyage count jumping from 84 to 144. Further support for freight rates could come from discharge delays at Port Qasim, which handles more than 90% of Pakistan’s coal imports. Pakistan may not be alone in reassessing its energy mix.

items.title: Open letter on freedom of navigation and the protection of seafarers
items.original_title: Open letter on freedom of navigation and the protection of seafarers
items.summary: European Shipowners | ECSA, BIMCO, the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council (WSC) welcome and support the EU-led ‘Pledge on Maintaining the Integrity of the International Law of the Sea – No Fees/No Tolls’, announced on 12 October 2026. We commend the European Union, its Member States and partner countries for their united commitment to protecting freedom of navigation, which underpins global shipping and the carriage of around 90% of world trade. The pledge sends an important signal of international unity against the use of tolls or fees and restrictions affecting passage through straits used for international navigation. We share its commitment to preserving the legal framework established by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), rejecting coercive unilateral measures and strengthening multilateral cooperation, particularly through the International Maritime Organization (IMO). For our industry, the safety and protection of seafarers is a precondition of freedom of navigation. Seafarers are the backbone of global trade and must be able to carry out their work safely. Such efforts should be accompanied by sustained coordination between States, relevant naval forces and the shipping industry to help translate commitments to freedom of navigation into effective protection of seafarers and shipping at sea.

items.original_title: GPS Jamming Resilience: See Where AIS Positions Are Denied or Injected in Near Real Time
items.summary: GPS jamming is not a vessel doing something. It is outside interference, usually from a military source, affecting everything in range. Any vessel, aircraft, or phone in that area is hit regardless of flag, owner, or cargo. Injected AIS positions near Lesser Tunb pull vessel tracks into a tight loop around a single point, a pattern real traffic does not make. The Scale In the Middle East Gulf alone, since February 28, 2026, Windward has recorded 94,804 unique vessels affected by GPS jamming and more than 3.1 million false ship-to-ship meetings generated by injected coordinates. The timeline slider runs back 90 days, so you can see patterns and where the GPS jamming hotspots are. In the six days from February 28 to March 5, 2026, as GPS jamming in the Gulf intensified, Windward removed 2,056 port calls across 845 vessels and 20,848 meetings across 695 vessels. The model flagged spoofed positions around Callao across 18 days, peaking between October 9 and 11, and linked them back to the areas off Romania and Bulgaria where the vessels really were. Visibility into where GPS jamming actually occurred lets them keep the standard and ask the question only when it is warranted.

items.title: Danish Shipping: Poland’s additional national requirements distort competition
items.original_title: Danish Shipping: Poland’s additional national requirements distort competition
items.summary: Poland has introduced a national survey requirement for smaller foreign-flagged vessels operating in Polish waters. This creates significant costs and practical difficulties for Danish shipping companies looking to take on work in Poland. Danish Shipping is concerned that other countries may introduce similar requirements and has therefore raised the issue at EU level. Under a change in Polish law, Danish vessels under 500 GT without a SOLAS certificate must undergo a survey and obtain a specific Polish national certificate, even if they have already been approved by the Danish authorities or a classification society. ‘’ It is easy to suspect that protecting Polish shipping from international competition is a bigger concern than safety’’ Nina Porst, Executive Director for Sustainable Ships and Skills at Danish Shipping The additional Polish requirement undermines the established practice of countries recognising one another’s flag State certification and using port State control to check the condition of vessels. “The additional Polish requirements affect any foreign operator looking to take on work in Poland. If individual countries start imposing additional national requirements for the technical approval and certification of foreign-flagged vessels, others may follow suit. Danish Shipping opposes additional national requirements of this kind in areas already governed by international rules.

In that regard, we spoke with Oystein Kalleklev, Managing Director, Commercial – Gas, at EPS, to hear his perspectives on the vessel’s delivery, the opportunities and challenges of operating on ammonia, and what lies ahead, with additional technical insights from Mirtcho Spassov, Manager Decarbonisation, at EPS. Impact on EPS’s newbuilding programme How could the operational experience and lessons from Terra Clove influence EPS’s wider newbuilding programme and its approach to alternative-fuel vessels going forward? Terra Clove represents an important opportunity for EPS to be among the pioneers in developing the knowledge and capabilities needed to operate dual-fuel ammonia vessels, and we intend to leverage these learnings to guide future deployments across other vessel types. Sharing lessons with the industry Alongside the delivery of Terra Clove, EPS has entered a strategic partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping (Center).

items.title: China faces daunting shipbuilding arithmetic
items.original_title: China faces daunting shipbuilding arithmetic
items.summary: Chinese shipbuilders are scheduled to deliver more than three times as much bulk carrier and tanker tonnage in 2028 as they did last year, according to fresh research from Banchero Costa that raises further questions over the industry’s ability to make good on its record orderbook. Chinese yards are contracted to deliver 92.7m dwt of bulk carriers and tankers in 2028, against just 30.4m dwt last year and a previous annual record of 62.6m dwt set in 2011. Across the seven principal merchant shipping sectors tracked by the Italian shipbroker, the orderbook stood at 5,488 vessels totalling 172.3m compensated gross tonnes (cgt) at the end of October, up 24% year-on-year and some 31% above the previous 2007 peak recorded in its dataset. These yards delivered just 1m cgt last year but are scheduled to deliver 10.1m cgt in 2028, representing one-sixth of anticipated global output across these sectors. The Dalian shipbuilder, which only recommenced commercial deliveries in 2024, delivered 66 vessels in the opening 10 months of this year but is contracted to deliver 101 next year and an astonishing 193 in 2028. As reported by Splash earlier this month, research from Danish Ship Finance shows shipbuilding capacity has expanded by just 30% since 2020, while the orderbook has grown three and a half times.

items.title: From global energy policy to practical innovation: AET at COP31
items.original_title: From global energy policy to practical innovation: AET at COP31
items.summary: At COP31, AET President and CEO Nick Potter joined government and industry leaders to discuss how shipping can support the development of global clean-energy supply chains and attract the investment needed to bring them to market. As Co-chair of the Clean Energy Marine Hubs (CEM-Hubs) Steering Committee and Chair of its Private Sector Group, Nick brought AET’s experience as an energy logistics operator to discussions on future fuels, maritime investment, the infrastructure required to bring clean fuels to market and the conditions needed to achieve the Belém 4X Pledge. At a dedicated session on maritime electrification, Nick also presented AET’s work on electric propulsion, sharing what we’re learning and what is needed for wider adoption across the industry. For AET, these discussions are closely connected to the investments we’re making across our fleet, from LNG and ammonia dual-fuel tankers to hybrid-electric, ethanol-ready dual-fuel DPSTs and energy efficiency retrofits such as wind-assisted propulsion and electrification. This includes AET Innovator, the world’s longest-range plug-in hybrid-electric vessel, set to be unveiled on 1 December 2026 in New Orleans. These investments also reflect our approach to decarbonisation – pursuing multiple fuel and technology pathways, working with customers and technology partners to develop solutions that improve efficiency, are commercially viable and deliver meaningful emissions reductions.

items.title: Cosco looks forward to fleet expansion as revenue and profits rise
items.original_title: Cosco looks forward to fleet expansion as revenue and profits rise
items.summary: Cosco Shipping Lines is pushing ahead with one of the industry’s largest newbuilding programmes, seemingly unperturbed by overcapacity concerns. Currently, Cosco and subsidiary OOCL have ordered 100 vessels, for around 1.46m teu of new capacity, as well as leases for vessels under construction totalling around 500,000 teu, all scheduled for delivery by 2030. As at 30 September, the self-operated container fleet stood at 610 vessels, with total capacity of roughly 3.66m teu, which are deployed on 458 routes, calling at 676 ports in some 147 countries. For the first nine months of the year, Cosco Shipping Holdings’ revenue was up 12% year on year, at $28bn, while net profit was up 13%, to $4.65bn. During an online briefing to shareholders, Cosco representatives said: “Newbuilding decisions are grounded in rigorous analysis of trade trends and long-term capacity planning, not speculative ordering.” The company cited the key justifications as fleet renewal and modernisation, as environmental regulations tightened. “More than 22% of the existing global container fleet will be over 20 years old and likely slated for scrapping by 2028–2029.

items.title: BIMCO puts ship-to-ship transfer costs on charterers
items.original_title: BIMCO puts ship-to-ship transfer costs on charterers
items.summary: Shipping organisation BIMCO has released a new standard clause for tanker charterparties that places the costs and risks of ship-to-ship cargo transfers on charterers while preserving the master’s authority over vessel safety. Published this week, the clause covers conventional and gas tankers, including cargo transfers involving onshore and offshore installations. Under the wording, charterers ordering such operations will be responsible for the necessary equipment, regulatory permissions and associated expenses. Shipowners can also recover additional insurance premiums and other documented expenses arising from the operations, subject to prior approval from charterers. The clause allows owners to appoint a specialist mooring master or superintendent at the charterer’s expense when deemed necessary by the ship’s master. The provision was originally developed for BIMCO’s CO2TIME 2026 charterparty, adopted in April for the emerging liquefied carbon dioxide shipping market. BIMCO subsequently opted to make the clause available separately for wider use across the tanker sector. The organisation stressed that the provision does not address sanctions compliance and should be used alongside appropriate sanctions clauses where necessary.

items.title: Polish offshore wind rules draw Danish shipowner backlash
items.original_title: Polish offshore wind rules draw Danish shipowner backlash
items.summary: Danish shipowners have raised concerns at EU level over new Polish vessel certification requirements, warning that additional inspections are making it harder for foreign operators to compete for offshore wind and marine construction contracts in the Baltic Sea. Industry association Danish Shipping has challenged rules requiring certain foreign-flagged vessels below 500 gt to undergo additional technical surveys before working in Polish waters, even where they already hold certificates from their flag administrations. The requirements primarily affect crew transfer vessels (CTVs), which carry personnel and equipment to offshore wind farms, alongside smaller construction and support vessels. Under Poland’s revised Maritime Safety Act, foreign vessels not covered by the SOLAS convention that operate in relevant Polish waters for more than 14 days in a calendar year must obtain a national operating permit. Danish Shipping argued that the additional procedures duplicate existing flag-state oversight and create obstacles for companies seeking work on Poland’s expanding offshore wind projects. Chief executive Michael Normann said the rules were restricting the company’s access to the Polish market despite its existing operating experience in the country. Poland’s changes were introduced through amendments adopted in October 2025. Polish maritime legal specialists have linked the measures to concerns about insufficient technical oversight of some foreign-flagged vessels operating outside the main international convention framework.

items.title: Clean Port Coalition Urges EU to Accelerate Port Electrification
items.original_title: Clean Port Coalition Urges EU to Accelerate Port Electrification
items.summary: The Clean Port Coalition has written to the European Commission calling for ambitious EU rules to accelerate port electrification and shore power ahead of the AFIR review. Ahead of the upcoming Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) review, the Clean Port Coalition (CPC), an alliance of industry, civil society, and maritime and energy stakeholders, has sent a joint letter to the European Commission calling for ambitious rules to scale up port electrification and shore power. While welcoming the EU’s recent Ports Strategy and Electrification Action Plan, the coalition warns that overcoming grid bottlenecks, financing gaps, and regulatory uncertainty requires decisive policy action. • Provide a predictable regulatory horizon for the deployment of onshore power supply for all vessels calling at EU ports in the upcoming AFIR review, starting with the most operationally feasible segments. • Battery charging infrastructure: Introduce clear requirements to ensure sufficient charging capacity for Europe’s growing fleet of battery electric vessels. • Clean energy hubs: Streamline grid access and accelerate energy storage and flexibility measures to integrate ports into the wider electricity grid. Source: European Federation for Transport and Environment AISBL

items.title: Oil edges higher as Hormuz attacks threaten Persian Gulf supply recovery
items.original_title: Oil edges higher as Hormuz attacks threaten Persian Gulf supply recovery
items.summary: Oil prices edged higher in Asian trading on Thursday as renewed attacks on commercial vessels and Saudi energy infrastructure threatened to derail the recovery in crude shipments from the Persian Gulf, although rising U.S. inventories and expectations of a global supply surplus limited gains. As of 01:21 ET (06:21 GMT), Brent crude futures rose 0.6% to $95.13 a barrel, while U.S. Iran-aligned Houthi militants escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the Ras Tanura oil refinery and two Red Sea ports with four drones. ANZ analysts said the attacks threatened to interrupt the recovery in oil flows. Persian Gulf exports increased last week but remained on a declining trend, while Strait of Hormuz transits edged higher. Hormuz throughput remained at only 49% of normal levels, with low inventories and virtually no spare capacity leaving the market exposed to further disruptions, ANZ estimated. Higher imports and weaker exports contributed to the increase, with U.S. OPEC+ ministers meet on Sunday, November 29, to discuss 2027 production policy.

items.summary: Pacific International Lines (PIL) and Qingdao Port Group have marked a significant milestone in maritime decarbonisation with China’s first LBM bunkering operation for international shipping. This is the first LBM bunkering to an internationally-trading ship in China and marks Qingdao Port’s capability to offer green LNG molecules to international shipping lines. In this first phase, PIL is using it as a drop-in fuel for its LNG dual-fuel vessels without any modification to their machinery systems. It advances Qingdao Port’s development as a regional green bunkering hub. Our partnership with PIL reflects our shared commitment to maritime decarbonisation, and we will keep expanding renewable fuel options for international shipping.” Delivered to PIL in 2024, Kota Odyssey is an LNG dual-fuel container vessel deployed on PIL’s SWS service connecting Asia with West Africa.

items.summary: Harry Vafias-led StealthGas has wrapped up seven charter deals for its LPG carriers, lifting its contracted revenue backlog to $115m and securing employment for one vessel into 2030. The Japanese-built vessel has secured a three-year time charter extension through January 2030.StealthGas has also agreed one-year extensions for the Eco Galaxy, Gas Esco, Eco Stream, Eco Blizzard and Eco Chios , alongside a new one-year fixture for the 2007-built Gas Haralambos . The chartering push comes ahead of a significant fleet expansion at StealthGas. Earlier this month, the company struck a $254.6m deal to acquire four LPG carriers from companies linked to the Vafias family. The acquisition would increase the owner’s carrying capacity by 35% and remains subject to shareholder approval at a meeting scheduled for December 11. StealthGas said it intends to fund the purchases from its own resources, with cash and short-term investments currently exceeding $275m and its fleet free of bank debt.

items.summary: The European Parliament has voted against adding two Indian shipbreaking yards to the EU’s approved recycling list, drawing a sharp rebuke from BIMCO and dealing another setback to shipowners seeking greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. MEPs have backed an objection to the European Commission’s proposed inclusion of Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang shipbreaking hub in Gujarat, by 377 votes to 214, with 24 abstentions. The vote came a day after eight international shipping associations, including BIMCO, European Shipowners, the International Chamber of Shipping, INTERCARGO and INTERTANKO, urged lawmakers to support the Indian yards. The industry maintains that existing European recycling capacity is insufficient to handle the anticipated increase in larger merchant vessels heading for demolition over the coming decade. Environmental campaigners welcomed the result, arguing that the beaching method used in Alang cannot provide adequate protection against pollution and hazardous waste. Ingvild Jenssen, executive director of NGO Shipbreaking Platform, said the Commission must apply the same environmental and safety standards regardless of where yards are located. As previously reported by Splash , the Parliament’s environment committee backed the objection earlier this month, despite both facilities receiving preliminary approval from the Commission following inspections.

items.title: ETS for maritime revision – The EU must not miss the opportunity to protect its ports and maritime connectivity
items.original_title: ETS for maritime revision – The EU must not miss the opportunity to protect its ports and maritime connectivity
items.summary: Ahead of the European Parliament’s Environment Committee vote on the maritime EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), FEPORT, representing European private port companies and terminal operators, the European Transport Workers’ Federation (ETF), the European Shippers’ Council (ESC), CLECAT, representing freight forwarders and logistics providers, the European Community Association of Ship Brokers and Agents (ECASBA), the European Maritime Pilots’ Association (EMPA) and the European Tugowners’ Association (ETA) call on Parliament and Council to act. We cannot miss this opportunity to prevent transhipment traffic from shifting outside the EU and to protect fair competition and connectivity across European ports. The maritime EU ETS applies directly to shipping companies, but decisions about where ships call affect the entire port community. Competing ports can serve the same markets and hinterlands, yet the services calling at them could face different ETS costs because of the length of the voyage. ETS relief should be proportionate to the actual share of containers unloaded at an EU port for onward shipment to a non-EU port. This would target the cargo most exposed to relocation and avoid sharp changes in ETS costs at fixed cargo thresholds. Co-legislators should also consider applying the same principle to the subsequent outbound leg and covering container ships from 5,000 TEU, since some EU transhipment ports mainly serve vessels below 10,000 TEU.

He adds that some shipping lines have discharged UK-bound containers at European hub ports rather than their originally scheduled UK destinations, although the carriers have committed to recovery plans to move the affected containers on to their booked UK ports. Davies Turner says that customers must also consider European customs requirements, full upfront payment of release charges, the requirement to return empty containers to the mainland European port, and potential demurrage and detention costs.

items.title: Rough seas ahead? The HCC’s sector inquiry and the competition outlook for Greek coastal shipping
items.original_title: Rough seas ahead? The HCC’s sector inquiry and the competition outlook for Greek coastal shipping
items.summary: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, Greek coastal shipping has drawn significant attention from the HellenicCompetition Commission (HCC). The pandemic reduced passenger traffic and accelerated consolidation, bringing ticket prices, connectivity and the resilience of island services to the top of the public agenda. Over the past six years, the HCC has sanctioned anticompetitive conduct on specific routes, reviewed a major merger between ferry operators, raided other ferry operators on different routes, and most recently concluded a sector inquiry in coastal shipping. This article summarises the recent enforcement action in coastal shipping, the findings of the HCC’s sector inquiry, and what they mean for operators. The HCC considers that Greek coastal shipping comprises several distinct relevant markets, defined on a route-by-route basis, which are concentrated and shaped by seasonality, high entry barriers and infrastructure constraints. The group also called on shipping companies to remove their vessels from the area. The exchange follows a Houthi drone strike Tuesday on the tallest tower in Riyadh, which Saudi authorities said injured at least 11 people. Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and essential supplies into Houthi-controlled northern Yemen. The port has long served as a critical channel for humanitarian aid and commercial imports for millions of Yemenis in a country heavily dependent on imported goods. Clashes between the two sides have intensified since September, when the Houthis advanced toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping passage at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Since then, the Houthis have increased strikes on Saudi airports, ports, and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has stepped up airstrikes on Houthi positions inside Yemen. Source: Investing.com

items.title: IMO Sounds Alarm Over Shortage of Training Berths for Future Seafarers
items.original_title: IMO Sounds Alarm Over Shortage of Training Berths for Future Seafarers
items.summary: The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and the lack of opportunities for young people to gain the sea time required to enter the profession. In many developing countries, aspiring officers complete their shore-based maritime education only to spend years waiting for an onboard training placement, even as shipping companies struggle to recruit qualified personnel. In an announcement Tuesday, the IMO outlined efforts to expand its NextWave Seafarers initiative, which aims to address the bottleneck through cooperation between governments, shipowners and maritime training institutions. More than 80 participants representing over 25 countries gathered at IMO headquarters in London on November 20 to formally launch the second phase of the initiative and explore ways to increase the availability of onboard training opportunities. The second phase aims to train at least 30 additional cadets, with women accounting for half of participants. The IMO also wants to recruit at least five shipping companies to provide training berths, laying the groundwork for a wider international partnership. The workshop examined practical barriers to cadet placements, including visa restrictions complicating crew changes, as well as the importance of providing a safe and supportive working environment for young seafarers entering the industry.

items.title: Transportation bottlenecks and aggregate shocks
items.original_title: Transportation bottlenecks and aggregate shocks
items.summary: A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years. This column examines how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks, comparing the Commodity Supercycle of the 2000s and the post-pandemic Great Supply Chain Disruption. The spike in freight rates for dry bulk shipping in the former episode was due to scarce shipping capacity, while the latter stemmed from scarce port capacity. A barrage of transportation disruptions has affected the global economy in recent years, from the Great Supply Chain Disruption following the COVID-19 pandemic to disruptions in the Red Sea, environmental shocks in critical waterways, and recent tensions around the Strait of Hormuz. Ships carry more than 80% of world trade in goods, and transportation accounts for a substantial part of the time required to move inputs across countries. 2026), we study how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks. The Great Supply Chain Disruption: Ports became the bottleneck As shown in Figure 1, between 2013 and 2020, the transportation system generally had spare capacity. Effective port capacity declined, and by 2021, the port constraint became binding for several quarters. In a counterfactual in which transportation capacity is sufficiently high that the constraint does not bind, commodity price inflation between 2019 and 2021–23 is about three percentage points lower, accounting for roughly 13% of the observed increase.

items.title: USD ≈7bn lost per year: the hidden cost of how shipping trades
items.original_title: USD ≈7bn lost per year: the hidden cost of how shipping trades
items.summary: Shipping is no stranger to transformation. Changing engines, evolving crewing models and relocating shipbuilding all took costs out of moving cargo by sea. Torvald Klaveness believes the next shift is hiding in plain sight, in how cargo owners, operators, shipowners and ports contract and coordinate to harvest value from aligned incentives. From the cargo owner’s perspective, the study identifies and quantifies around USD 7bn a year in potentially avoidable costs across dry bulk and product tanker shipping. Klaveness believes the full potential could reach USD 10–20bn a year, or 5–10% of the roughly USD 190bn spent on freight in the two segments. The study reviewed around 50 possible sources of inefficiency and examined 14 in depth, so roughly half of the potential is still to be explored. The USD 7bn is an indicative sum of individual estimates, with some overlap, and is not a savings forecast. Over the years, we have sensed that significant value is lost every day in how decisions are made across companies. That is the opportunity, and no single company can or should capture it alone.” The portfolio companies in which Torvald Klaveness has active ownership in have worked on aspects of trading efficiency for years, but lacked a clear picture of how big the problem was, or whether long-standing industry norms could realistically change.

Tightening port pollution rules would save society billions and protect the health of port communities, says T&E. According to the report, removing loopholes in the EU rules would save Europe €1.56bn in health and climate costs. items.summary: A new technical and commercial assessment of 200,000m³ LNG carrier concepts, produced by LR Advisory for GTT and presented at Gastech 2026, suggests the industry may be approaching a useful middle ground, where vessels are significantly larger than the conventional 174,000m³ LNG carrier, but still capable of accessing much of the existing global terminal network. 200,000 vs 174,000 LR analysis compared representative 200,000m³ designs with a 174,000m³ LNG carrier, examining terminal accessibility alongside representative commercial Atlantic and Pacific operating scenarios. It found that a 200,000m³ vessel could access approximately 88 LNG terminals globally, compared with 97 for its 174,000m³ counterpart. Rather than requiring a fundamental rebuilding of the LNG terminal network, a 200,000m³ vessel could potentially operate across many of the trades already central to the global LNG market. “Our analysis shows that 200,000m³ LNG carriers can retain access to most major LNG terminals while increasing cargo carrying capacity, making them a practical option for owners looking to improve transportation efficiency and support future trade growth.” The issue is relevant to fleet renewal as the assessment notes an ageing LNG carrier fleet requiring replacement alongside growing LNG trade volumes, strong shipyard orderbooks and demand for more efficient vessel designs.

SCI is separately seeking to acquire up to four secondhand containerships ranging from 1,500 to 2,500 TEU in capacity. The government has been courting major South Korean shipbuilders, including HD Hyundai, Samsung Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean, to invest in domestic shipbuilding capacity.

The latest warnings from United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) detail attacks against three tankers and a bulk carrier on November 22, underscoring the persistent threat to commercial shipping nearly nine months into the Iran war. Meanwhile, Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) announced that it had added 26 tugboats to its list of non-compliant vessels, accusing them of providing services to ships operating in violation of its restrictions in the southern Strait of Hormuz. The latest attacks come as the International Maritime Organization’s tally of confirmed maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and wider Middle East reached 141 as of November 23, with 25 confirmed seafarer fatalities. According to JMIC, 114 vessels completed U.S.-facilitated transits between November 19 and 21, averaging 38 per day, up from 27 per day during the preceding four days.

items.title: Grounded bulker pulled free off French coast
items.original_title: Grounded bulker pulled free off French coast
items.summary: Salvors have successfully refloated the 28,200 dwt bulk carrier Miro G , four days after the ship was driven onto a beach on France’s Atlantic coast. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged bulker was pulled clear of the shoreline at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe, on Tuesday afternoon by Les Abeilles International’s emergency response tug Abeille Bretagne. The vessel is set to be towed north to Le Verdon, at the mouth of the Gironde estuary, according to Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul, who confirmed that no pollution had been detected. Salvors took advantage of improving sea conditions and a rising tide, pumping ballast water out of the 169-m-long bulker to reduce its draught before pulling it free using a 1,900-m high-strength synthetic towline. Shallow waters had prevented the tug from approaching within about 900 m of the stranded vessel. As reported by Splash on Monday, the Miro G ran aground early on Friday after gusts of up to 48 knots caused it to drag its anchors. Nineteen of the vessel’s 22 crew were airlifted to safety on Friday, with the remaining three evacuated alongside salvage personnel on Saturday ahead of deteriorating weather. The bulker was carrying around 100 tonnes of fuel when it ran aground. items.title: Used Supertankers Now Cost More Than New Ships as Hormuz War Upends Shipping Markets
items.original_title: Used Supertankers Now Cost More Than New Ships as Hormuz War Upends Shipping Markets
items.summary: The war with Iran has so severely distorted the global oil tanker market that 15-year-old supertankers are now worth considerably more than brand-new vessels, highlighting the extraordinary premium placed on immediately available shipping capacity. Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH revealed Tuesday in its third-quarter earnings report that the market value of a 15-year-old very large crude carrier (VLCC) has reached $165 million, some 25% above the $132 million price of ordering a new vessel, according to Clarksons data. The valuation is more than three-and-a-half times the 10-year average of $46 million for a tanker of that age. CMB.TECH estimates that 141 tankers are now dedicated exclusively to shuttling crude and petroleum products, with VLCCs accounting for 72% of those vessels. The global VLCC orderbook now stands at 33.1% of the existing fleet, while the Suezmax orderbook has reached 29.3%, according to Clarksons data presented by CMB.TECH. An eventual normalization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could release significant tanker capacity back into the international market, potentially coinciding with a wave of newbuilding deliveries in the coming years. For now, the fact that a 15-year-old supertanker commands a $33 million premium over a new vessel illustrates just how valuable existing shipping capacity has become in a world at war.

items.title: Flexibility the ‘real commercial value’ for shippers facing disruption
items.original_title: Flexibility the ‘real commercial value’ for shippers facing disruption
items.summary: Shippers risk undermining their supply chain resilience by awarding transport contracts primarily on price, with increasingly little protection offered by logistics operators when costs rise or capacity constraints hinder movements. Chris Clowes, executive director of Scala, said while companies often sought to diversify transport suppliers to reduce exposure to disruption, that approach could create a false sense of security if providers are operating on commercially unsustainable rates. He told The Loadstar : “Having two transport providers on a particular lane may look like sensible contingency planning, but if both have won business by bidding at unsustainably low rates in a procurement exercise, how resilient is the arrangement? Logistics decision-makers should consider the commercial sustainability of suppliers, as well as their operational capability.” Rather than judging resilience on the number of suppliers they use, Mr Clowes said shippers needed to assess just how genuinely independent and commercially viable their alternative arrangements were. He argued that procurement decisions should account for the financial sustainability of logistics providers alongside their operational capabilities, noting the issue reflects a wider problem with how companies approach supply chain resilience.

Andrii Sybiha said that both Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment were valid targets and Ukraine’s right to self-defense was enshrined in the United Nations charter, Article 51. We emphasize that Ukraine’s actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people.” International law does not limit the right to self-defense to the territory where the aggression takes place: it can be on the territory of the aggressor, or in international waters, Sybiha said. items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Maersk and ONE tipped to create first global north-south alliance
items.original_title: EXCLUSIVE: Maersk and ONE tipped to create first global north-south alliance
items.summary: The formation of container shipping’s first global liner alliance covering the north-south trades appears to be taking shape, The Loadstar has learned. Container lines have traditionally treated the north-south trades as a set of separate marriages, on the assumption that the right partner depends on the trade. However, according to sources in Asia, Maersk and Ocean Network Express (ONE) are working to develop a vessel-sharing agreement (VSA) covering the trades globally, rather than lane by lane. Their respective groupings, the Gemini Cooperation for Maersk and Premier Alliance for ONE, stop at east-west trades, while north-south has remained a patchwork of classic VSAs, where each carrier’s slots follow the ships it provides, and an agreement rarely covers more than two or three services. In that context, it is worth noting that Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd do not cooperate on any of their respective Asia-WC South America services – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Maersk operates two standalone strings, the AC1 and AC3, while Hapag-Lloyd’s three offerings are run in cooperation with MSC, HMM, and ONE. On Far East–WC South America, for example, Linerlytica puts Maersk at 16.1% of weekly capacity and ONE at 9%; together a quarter of the trade, ahead of CMA CGM and MSC, from two carriers whose customers overlap less.

items.title: Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies
items.original_title: Torvald Klaveness puts $7bn price tag on shipping inefficiencies
items.summary: Norwegian shipping group Torvald Klaveness has identified around $7bn in potential annual savings across dry bulk and product tanker shipping, with excessive transaction costs, underutilised vessels and poor port coordination among the industry’s biggest sources of inefficiency. The Oslo-based company’s new study, examining approximately $190bn in annual freight spending across the two sectors, suggests the wider opportunity could be worth between $10bn and $20bn a year. The research examined around 50 potential sources of inefficiency, with 14 investigated in detail using voyage data, market benchmarks and operational evidence. Another $1.4bn could be unlocked by deploying larger vessels on trades currently served by smaller ships, while better use of available cargo capacity represents a further $1bn opportunity. Klaveness calculates that around $700m could potentially be saved by improving vessel arrival times, reducing the practice of ships steaming at higher speeds only to wait at anchor for a berth. Klaveness also identified around $400m in potential fuel savings from addressing misaligned incentives in time-charter contracts, where shipowners may have limited financial motivation to invest in efficiency improvements because charterers pay for the fuel. Other costs include an estimated $300m from claims and disputes, while unreliable shipping schedules could be adding between $300m and $700m annually to the financing costs of excess inventories held by dry bulk importers.

items.title: UN urges probe after Russian ship attacked off Libya
items.original_title: UN urges probe after Russian ship attacked off Libya
items.summary: The United Nations called on Monday (Nov 23) for an independent probe into drone attacks on two ships off Libya, including a Russian vessel, in a suspected spillover from the Ukraine war. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for either strike on Sunday off the port city of Benghazi, but they came as Ukrainian forces stepped up attacks against Russia far from the front lines. The UN mission in Libya expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. Authorities said all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment for minor injuries after drones hit a Russian ship and another vessel, without specifying where it was from. Libya Alhadath television reported later that naval and air force units intercepted more than 12 “explosive-laden sea drones” off Benghazi. The attacks came after a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday, close to the waters of Finland, whose border guard said the strike was Ukrainian. “It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones,” an official statement said. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack, which Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed on Ukraine.

items.original_title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia’s Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard. It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments. The company says it was established within the structure of Russia’s defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex. Finland’s coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.” Shortly after the incident, Finland’s defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country’s airspace, potentially linked to “rescue or tracking operations”.

items.title: Battery Vessels Could Help Electrify Most of Global Shipping Emissions
items.original_title: Battery Vessels Could Help Electrify Most of Global Shipping Emissions
items.summary: Battery-electric ships are economical only if the pack is cycled frequently, so they have been confined to short-sea, ferry and harbour vessels rather than the infrequently-berthing deep-sea fleet. Dedicated battery vessels (BVs) remove this limit by separating the battery from the host: coupling at or near a port and returning to port to recharge, they keep their packs cycling across many hosts. Using a gridded shipping- CO2 field and a geometric relay-corridor servability model, we map the global share BVs could serve. On a denominator of all shipping CO2(e), the battery-addressable share is about 62%, its servable corridors concentrated in European–Mediterranean and East and Southeast Asian waters. A screening cost model puts BV-delivered energy at breakeven with fuel oil near $173/tCO2e (well-to-wake basis) for a 20MW host and a future $100/kWh battery pack price, falling as host power rises. The maritime economy enters the latter part of 2026 after another period of disruption and adjustment. It carries more than 80% of world trade by volume¹ and remains the most energy-efficient way to move goods over long distances. Its ability to adapt has again demonstrated the central role of maritime transport in the global economy. Global goods trade reached approximately USD 13.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, an increase of 12.5% compared with the same period in 2025.

items.title: Tianjin Southwest Maritime takes delivery of China-built ammonia-capable gas carrier

items.summary: The 25,000-cbm vessel can use its ammonia cargo as fuel and has a pre-fitted ammonia bunkering connection. Tianjin Southwest Maritime took delivery of the gas carrier André M from CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding this month, China Classification Society (CCS) said. The vessel can switch between ammonia and conventional fuel oil. CCS called it the first ammonia dual-fuel gas carrier built in China and the third of its kind worldwide. No rules covered ammonia cargo as fuel on gas carriers when the project started in early 2024, CCS said. This development follows the delivery of two ammonia-capable gas carriers from HD Hyundai to Belgian shipping firm Exmar earlier this year. Its first, Antwerpen, used part of its ammonia cargo as fuel on its maiden voyage, so it needed no separate bunkering operation, Kristof Coppé, director of fleet operations and technical business development at Exmar, told ENGINE. CCS did not say where André M will trade. Source: By Tuhin Roy, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/

items.title: World Shipping Council calls for global agreement on shipping emissions as industry investment surpasses $200 billion USD
items.original_title: World Shipping Council calls for global agreement on shipping emissions as industry investment surpasses $200 billion USD
items.summary: The World Shipping Council (WSC) is calling on governments to agree on binding global greenhouse gas regulations for international shipping without further delay, warning that continued uncertainty risks slowing investment in cleaner fuels and infrastructure. As the next round of negotiations get underway at the International Maritime Organization (IMO), WSC has identified three elements it considers essential to an effective agreement that delivers on the commitments governments made under the 2023 GHG Strategy: • A credible pathway to net zero, with clear and predictable emissions reduction requirements aligned with the IMO’s 2023 GHG Strategy’s ambition. Representing the global commercial shipping fleet, the associations urged governments to agree on effective and enforceable global regulations that provide investment certainty, incentivise cleaner fuels and maintain a level playing field across international shipping. Container shipping and vehicle carriers have committed more than USD $200 billion to over 1,350 dual-fuel ships, including over 500 already operating. An agreement that delivers all three can accelerate progress towards net zero and help turn the investment already underway into real emissions reductions.” WSC cautions that further delays or a framework focused primarily on experience building or fuel market readiness would prolong uncertainty rather than support the transition.

items.title: HMM signs green shipping deal with Nextpower
items.original_title: HMM signs green shipping deal with Nextpower
items.summary: South Korean shipping company HMM said Monday it had signed a deal allowing US solar technology company Nextpower to reflect emissions reductions from HMM’s use of lower-carbon marine fuels in its supply chain emissions reporting. Under its Green Sailing Service, HMM uses lower-carbon fuels and passes the resulting emissions reductions on to cargo customers for use in their Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain. The agreements allow HMM to recover part of the cost of using lower-carbon fuels, helping fund further investments in lower-emission shipping. Reductions made to comply with regulations, including those in the European Union, are ineligible. HMM uses independent third-party verification to check the reported reductions and help avoid double counting, which occurs when more than one company claims the same reduction. Customers can use the verified figures in their environmental, social and governance disclosures. The Nextpower agreement follows similar deals with German logistics company Hellmann in 2023, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea in 2024 and US sportswear company Nike in 2025. We plan to continue investing in greenhouse gas reductions, including diversifying our use of low-carbon fuels,” an HMM official said. “We aim to develop our environmental initiatives into a new driver of growth.” Source: The Korea Heralde

items.title: ATEX compliance doesn’t end at delivery, and neither does the liability
items.original_title: ATEX compliance doesn’t end at delivery, and neither does the liability
items.summary: ATEX (ATmosphères EXplosibles), derived from EU Directive 2014/34/EU, governs equipment used in potentially explosive environments: tankers, barges, bunkering units, and any vessel handling hydrocarbons or flammable cargoes. Its requirements extend across design, manufacture, and maintenance – covering the entire operational life of equipment installed in hazardous areas, not just the moment it leaves the yard. This distinction matters because compliance can be lost in service, often without any visible change in equipment performance. Under the ADN inland waterway rules this is set out explicitly, and servicing by a company without ATEX certification can break compliance even where the work itself is sound, because the equipment can no longer be shown to meet the standard it was certified against. As charterer expectations around safety compliance tighten and port state control scrutiny increases globally, ATEX certification is increasingly relevant to commercial credibility as much as regulatory standing. Closing the compliance gap requires a structured approach to lifecycle management: certified service providers, genuine OEM parts, traceable documentation, and a forward-looking view of upgrade and recertification requirements. For fleet operators with older vessels, the 2034 deadline makes this especially pressing – yard availability and specialist resource will be constrained as the deadline approaches.

A framework including a global fuel standard and a pricing mechanism on greenhouse gas emissions from ships was already approved by IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee in spring 2025. Is there a fresh chance to get a global deal on shipping by the end of 2026? Shipping moves more than 80 per cent of global trade by volume and is responsible for 2.3 per cent of global CO2 emissions, roughly the same as the entire annual emissions of Japan. “Wind assisted propulsion systems and on-board carbon capture could save up to a further 25 per cent of GHG emissions.” Wind-power assisted propulsion systems, such as rotor sails, suction sails or wing sails, could bring down GHG emissions by up to 30 per cent per nautical mile – if weather and wind conditions are favourable. Central to the operation is a 1,900-meter (6,234-foot) towline being prepared aboard the French emergency towing vessel Abeille Bretagne. The favorable tidal trend is expected to continue through Thursday, November 26. The MIRO G ran aground during the night of November 19–20 after encountering strong winds and heavy seas off Lit-et-Mixe. On Friday, November 20, the French maritime prefect ordered the shipowner to take all necessary measures to arrange the vessel’s refloating as quickly as possible, while ensuring the safety of personnel and protection of the marine environment. The operation remains without a confirmed start date, with authorities seeking to balance the urgency of freeing the vessel against the risks of undertaking a difficult salvage operation in unfavorable conditions.

items.summary: Underlying growth in African airfreight demand is proving more significant than temporary benefits provided by shippers switching from ocean services, as expanding trade and new cargo flows create longer-term opportunities for the sector, according to Kenya Airways. The carrier acknowledged to The Loadstar that congestion, geopolitical uncertainty, and unreliable shipping schedules had encouraged some business to move cargo to airfreight, but said this was only one element of a broader increase in demand. “Some of the recent growth has been linked to temporary market conditions, including supply chain disruptions, seasonal cargo peaks, geopolitical developments, and capacity constraints in competing transport modes,” said a spokesperson. Kenya Airways identified expanding consumer markets, population growth, urbanisation, industrialisation, and increased regional integration through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as factors supporting sustained demand for air cargo. Citing increasing demand on Africa-Europe, Africa-Middle East, Africa-Asia, and intra-African trade corridors, the spokesperson noted that Nairobi was positioned as a gateway connecting East, Central, Southern and West Africa with international markets. “Collectively, these trends position African air cargo for continued growth in the years ahead,” the spokesperson noted, highlighting emerging cargo categories, pointing to increased movement of solar panels and related equipment destined for the US.

items.title: Russia’s Northern Sea Route Breaks 40 Million-Tonne Barrier For First Time, but Putin’s Ambitions Remain Out of Reach
items.original_title: Russia’s Northern Sea Route Breaks 40 Million-Tonne Barrier For First Time, but Putin’s Ambitions Remain Out of Reach
items.summary: Nuclear icebreaker Vaygach escorting a convoy of crude oil and oil product tankers along the Northern Sea Route in July 2024. (Source: Atomflot) Cargo volumes along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) have surpassed 40 million tonnes for the first time, setting a new record for the Arctic shipping corridor. The milestone marks continued growth in Russian Arctic shipping, although volumes remain far below the ambitious targets set forth by President Vladimir Putin over the past decade. Over the past five years, annual cargo volumes have increased from 34.87 million tonnes in 2021 to more than 40 million tonnes in 2026, an increase of roughly 15%. The figures underline the NSR’s growing importance to Russia’s Arctic economy, but also show that recent growth has been relatively modest compared with the rapid expansion earlier in the decade. Putin set a target of 80 million tonnes of annual cargo traffic by 2024 in a 2018 presidential decree. The Centre for High North Logistics estimated that transit cargo totaled approximately 3.7 million tonnes by the end of September, with the season potentially exceeding 4.5 million tonnes if ongoing voyages were completed . The Oslo-listed company has signed a memorandum of agreement with Singapore-based Global Pacific Shipping for the 56,361 dwt bulker, with delivery scheduled between November 25 and December 30. The deal marks a second attempt to sell the ship after a previous agreement with Hong Kong’s Xing Le Investments collapsed in January. Jinhui had agreed to sell Jin Bi for $14.4m in December 2025, but the transaction was cancelled the following month after a contractual condition relating to timely delivery could not be met. Unlike the previous arrangement, which included $7m payable over four years, Global Pacific will pay the full purchase price before delivery. Jinhui said it expects to book a gain of approximately $5.2m on the sale, based on the vessel’s carrying value of $12.6m at the end of September. Last month, the company agreed to sell the 2007-built, 55,496 dwt Jin Xing for $14.6m, continuing its clearout of older supramax tonnage.

Brent has fallen roughly 20% this month after Trump held back from renewed strikes against Iran following the U.S. The International Energy Agency expects the global oil market to record a surplus of roughly 2 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter as recovering Persian Gulf exports outpace demand. Goldman Sachs has also highlighted the possibility of a substantial supply glut in 2027, as Middle Eastern production recovers and additional export infrastructure helps producers move crude around shipping bottlenecks.

items.summary: The LNG market remained under pressure this week, with an abundance of prompt vessel availability in the Atlantic continuing to weigh on freight rates. Close to around 10 cargoes were fixed or worked for the upcoming month, steadily absorbing available tonnage and tightening the position list. items.title: How the oil market could move from famine to glut
items.original_title: How the oil market could move from famine to glut
items.summary: The constraint of Gulf crude exports since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March pushed Brent prices above US$100/bbl for much of the past nine months, triggering soaring fuel prices, rising inflation and weaker economic growth. Senior VP Alan Gelder and the wider WoodMac Macro Oils team foresee the potential for much lower prices when flows of exports resume on a peace agreement, reversing these knock-on effects. Additional supply is set to arrive on the market that could contribute to prices trading below our previous long-term forecasts well into the early 2030s. Crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz normalise progressively through 2027, allowing fundamentals to play a greater role in shaping the market once again. Whenever peace comes – by the end of the year in our Base Case or later as in the scenario – an agreement ending the threat to flows through the Strait could mark a shift from famine to glut. Holding substantial volumes off the market was a material factor in Brent averaging US$90/bbl from 2021 to 2025. Oil and gas companies are looking to strengthen portfolios to offset production declines in the mid-2030s. A dip in oil prices could present M&A opportunities for the financially strong.

items.title: US firm partners with SHI for nuclear-powered LNG carrier

items.summary: US-based nuclear technology firm Tesser Atomics has partnered with South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) to develop a nuclear-powered LNG carrier for transatlantic voyages. Under the memorandum of understanding, Samsung Heavy Industries will contribute its vessel design and construction expertise. Tesser Atomics will provide nuclear reactor technology and expertise in regulatory licensing for marine applications. Tesser describes its reactor as a “compact fluoride-salt-cooled high-temperature reactor (FHR) designed for ships”. The technology combines tristructural isotropic (TRISO) fuel with a low-pressure molten salt coolant in a small modular nuclear reactor. “Demonstrating nuclear propulsion on an LNG carrier crossing the Atlantic would open new horizons for decarbonizing the shipping industry,” Samsung Heavy Industries executive vice president Kyunghee Kim said. The project aims to demonstrate the commercial viability of nuclear-powered merchant ships and provide shipowners with evidence to inform future vessel investment decisions, Kim added. The companies have not disclosed a timeline for the vessel’s development or construction. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/

items.title: UBS flags resilient commodity investment case despite easing oil supply premium
items.original_title: UBS flags resilient commodity investment case despite easing oil supply premium
items.summary: UBS sees continued investment opportunities in critical minerals and power infrastructure as rising electricity demand, artificial intelligence spending, and electrification support long-term growth, even as technology-sector volatility raises concerns about valuations. In a November 16 research note, UBS said structural demand for electricity and digital infrastructure remains a major investment theme, supporting opportunities across grid modernization, renewable energy, nuclear power and industrial automation. The bank expects annual investment in power and related infrastructure to reach $3 trillion by 2030, driven partly by expanding data center capacity. Still, substantial investment pipelines and strong order backlogs support its longer-term outlook for companies exposed to electrification and power demand. UBS estimates overall AI-related capital expenditure will reach $1 trillion in 2026 before climbing to $1.4 trillion in 2027. UBS recommends diversified exposure across the AI value chain rather than concentrated positions in individual companies. Beyond technology and energy infrastructure, the bank identifies healthcare innovation as another long-term investment opportunity. It forecasts the global longevity market could generate $8 trillion in annual revenue by 2030, compared with $5.3 trillion in 2023. UBS favors targeted exposure to AI, power and resources, and longevity within diversified equity portfolios, balancing structural growth opportunities against sector-specific risks.

items.original_title: Tanker boom turns conservative owners into asset traders
items.summary: Surging tanker and VLGC values are turning some of shipping’s most conservative owners into opportunistic asset players, with a string of recent sales generating extraordinary returns in a matter of months. The disruption caused by the Strait of Hormuz crisis has sent secondhand values soaring, creating lucrative opportunities for owners and traders who acquired ships before prices took off. Malaysia’s MISC, traditionally regarded as one of shipping’s more conservative owners, is reportedly selling the 21-year-old shuttle tanker Jasmine Knutsen to Indonesian interests. In September, Trafigura Maritime acquired the Samsung-built suezmax Seaways Sabine from International Seaways for approximately $74m, some $53m above what the US-listed owner originally paid for the vessel when new. Just two months later, the same tanker, renamed Sponde, was reported sold again for around $110m. If confirmed, the transaction would deliver Trafigura a gross gain of approximately $36m in barely eight weeks. BW has also joined the selling spree, recently offloading the 83,134 cu m VLGC BW Mistral for well over $100m. Acquired as part of BW’s purchase of John Fredriksen-controlled Avance Gas’s VLGC fleet less than two years ago, the vessel is understood to have generated a gain of approximately $37m. With secondhand values reaching exceptional levels, the distinction between traditional shipowners and speculative asset traders is becoming increasingly blurred.

items.title: Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers
items.original_title: Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers
items.summary: Spain has become the latest country to clamp down on ship scrubbers, announcing a nationwide ban on washwater discharges in ports and designated coastal waters from July 1, 2027. Unlike countries that have initially targeted open-loop systems, Spain’s new royal decree covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid scrubbers from day one. The restrictions apply to all merchant vessels, regardless of flag, operating in Spanish internal maritime waters, port areas and designated anchorages within territorial waters. Ships will not have to remove their scrubbers but must switch to compliant low-sulphur fuel or retain wastewater onboard for subsequent disposal ashore. Spain’s decision goes beyond last year’s OSPAR agreement, which requires northeast Atlantic countries to ban open-loop discharges in ports and internal waters by July 2027, extending to all scrubber types in 2029. Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges in their territorial waters in July 2025, with restrictions on closed-loop systems following in 2029. Greenland’s parliament voted last month to introduce a phased ban, starting in July 2027. Scrubbers have become increasingly controversial since the IMO’s global sulphur cap took effect in 2020. Spain says scrubber washwater can contain heavy metals and organic pollutants and contribute to marine acidification.

items.original_title: Goldman Sachs: Oil Is Estimated to Ease in 2027 as Suppliers Adapt to Hormuz Disruption
items.summary: Oil is forecast to ease gradually in 2027 as suppliers in the Middle East adapt to disruption from the war in Iran, according to Goldman Sachs Research. What is the prediction for oil prices in 2027? Our commodities analysts expect benchmark Brent crude to average $88 per barrel in 2027 under their base case assumption of no definitive diplomatic breakthrough in Iran and no re-escalation with major long-term damage to oil infrastructure. Under Goldman Sachs Research’s base case scenario, our analysts expect the surplus to grow in 2027. Goldman Sachs Research expects an additional 3.8mb/d of pipeline capacity to come online over the next year as oil producers in the Middle East invest in pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport oil directly to the Gulf of Oman, Red Sea, or Mediterranean Sea. Goldman Sachs Research expects global demand, with the exception of China, to recover to its pre-war trend once the availability and affordability of oil products improve, consistent with the rebounds in global demand following negative oil supply shocks in 2011 and 2022. In China, our analysts expect persistent weakness in road fuel oil demand to drive 0.4 million barrels per day of “scarring” to global oil demand by the fourth quarter of 2027.

items.title: Two Supply Lines, One Terminal: 12 Sanctioned Tankers at the Houthi-Controlled Ras Issa
items.original_title: Two Supply Lines, One Terminal: 12 Sanctioned Tankers at the Houthi-Controlled Ras Issa
items.summary: Between September 16 and November 7, 2026, Windward MIOC identified 12 sanctioned tankers delivering fuel to Ras Issa, the Houthi-controlled oil terminal on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, together carrying an estimated 3.26 million barrels. Tracing the cargo back from the terminal, Windward found two distinct supply lines, one carrying Russian diesel and other fuels south through the Suez Canal, and one carrying Iranian-origin cargo out of the Middle East Gulf. The two supply lines Windward identified into Ras Issa run north from Russia via Suez and south from Iran via Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. What Happened Twelve Sanctioned Tankers, Eleven of Them Dark Across the seven-week window, Windward identified 12 sanctioned tankers at the Houthi-controlled Ras Issa terminal and the nearby Salif anchorage. Cargo on two of the tankers reached Ras Issa through chains of ship-to-ship transfers. One case illustrates the pattern end to end: On June 9, about 130,400 barrels of Russian diesel was loaded at Taman onto a Russian-flagged tanker sanctioned under Russia programs. Between September 11 and 20, the cargo passed through three ship-to-ship transfers, one off Port Said and two in the Gulf of Suez, each between Russian-flagged tankers sanctioned under Russia programs.

items.title: Spain to ban all scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports
items.original_title: Spain to ban all scrubber wastewater discharge in its ports
items.summary: Spain has banned ships from discharging wastewater from any type of scrubber in its ports and anchorages from 1 July 2027 to protect the marine environment, the transport ministry said. Spain’s Council of Ministers approved the royal decree on Tuesday. It applies to all civilian ships fitted with scrubbers, whatever their flag, and covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid systems alike. Spain’s move complies with the OSPAR Commission’s decision agreed in June last year, under which 15 European governments and the EU agreed to stop ships from discharging scrubber washwater in ports and internal waters. Each OSPAR member must ban discharges from open-loop scrubbers in internal waters and ports by 1 July 2027, and from scrubbers in any mode by 1 July 2029. Spain’s decision brings forward the ban on closed-loop and hybrid scrubbers by two years and extends the ban to areas outside those covered by the OSPAR decision. Class society DNV said in July last year that whether to extend the ban to the Mediterranean would be up to Spain and France. There are currently 7,230 ships equipped with scrubbers across the world, with the number expected to increase to 7,612 vessels by 2029, according to DNV data. Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges in their territorial waters from 1 July 2025.

items.title: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement
items.original_title: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement
items.summary: Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels. China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios. Key findings • The RNR policy would accelerate fleet renewal and result in additional NCEVs being introduced into the fleet. • Increasing the subsidy level without other supporting policies would lead to up to 17.4% higher well-to-wake greenhouse gas emissions between 2025 and 2050. • Combining a carbon pricing mechanism, an e-fuel blending mandate, and incentive support for e-fuels would help to jumpstart both NCEV adoption and e-fuel uptake.

Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October.
