items.title: Congestion at transhipment hubs keeps intra-Asia rates firm
items.original_title: Congestion at transhipment hubs keeps intra-Asia rates firm
items.summary: Worsening bottlenecks in South-east Asian ports have resulted in intra-Asia rates moving up, even as congestion in China eases. Yesterday, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) edged up $4 from 12 November, to $1,444 per 40ft, Shanghai-Manila rates rose 7%, to $1,310 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Laem Chabang increased 2%. to $1,584 per 40ft. Congestion intensified at major transhipment hubs, particularly Singapore, pushing rates from Shanghai to the port up 1%, to $2,064 per 40ft. Shanghai-Busan prices fell 8%, to $990 per 40ft, while Shanghai-Kaohsiung rates fell 3%, to $1,257 per 40ft, as average vessel waiting times decreased by three hours at Busan and four hours at Kaohsiung. Ahead of the peak season for intra-Asia shipping, carriers have been deploying more capacity. The PHX service will see Panstar deploying the 700 teu Dongjin Fortune , which will be chartered from compatriot feeder operator Dong Jin Shipping, and complements Pan-Continental’s 1,000 teu Pancon Harmony . Panstar plans to replace the Dongjin Fortune with a 1,000 teu chartered vessel next year. Panstar started out in liner shipping in 2024, with a South Korea-Japan feeder service.

items.summary: Deal Brings Yearly Tally to 47 Vessels and $8.54 Billion, Emphasizing Eco-Friendly High-Value Ships Hanwha Ocean has won an order for two Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) from a shipowner in Oceania. In a regulatory filing on Nov. 19, Hanwha Ocean said it had signed a shipbuilding contract worth a total of 364.2 billion won ($262.06 million). Including this contract, Hanwha Ocean has recorded orders for a total of 47 vessels (cases) so far this year. Its cumulative order value has reached about $8.54 billion, a solid trend that exceeds market expectations. The tally includes 24 VLCCs, eight liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, six container ships, three Very Large Ammonia Carriers (VLACs), and three Very Large Gas Carriers (VLGCs). In particular, the orders are led by eco-friendly vessels aligned with the carbon-neutral trend, special-purpose ships, and Wind Turbine Installation Vessels (WTIVs), all of which require highly advanced shipbuilding technology. Industry experts say Hanwha Ocean is focusing on selectively winning orders centered on high-profit vessel types rather than simply expanding order volume. The VLCC market requires high technological entry barriers and large-scale facilities, and Hanwha Ocean is solidifying its market dominance based on accumulated construction experience.

items.summary: Oslo-listed Hunter Group has launched a NOK1.63bn ($168m) takeover bid for Norwegian offshore accommodation player Jacktel, looking to put its windfall from lucrative VLCC charter contracts into a longer-term business. The bid has already secured commitments from six major Jacktel shareholders controlling around 73% of the company, including investment vehicles linked to chairman Harald Thorstein and Hunter board member Morten Astrup. The offer was initially set to expire at 9 am Oslo time on November 20, with the option of extending the deadline to November 23. Jacktel owns the four-legged, self-elevating accommodation rig Haven , which can house up to 444 offshore personnel and has been deployed on major North Sea oil and gas developments. The unit is currently working for Aker BP at the Valhall field, where its firm contract runs until February 2028, with options potentially extending employment through June that year. Jacktel reported 100% utilisation during the third quarter, generating $19m in revenue and $10.3m in EBITDA.

items.title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.original_title: India scraps compulsory retirement age for ships
items.summary: India has scrapped compulsory retirement ages for ships flying its flag, reversing a policy designed to push older tonnage out of the country’s merchant fleet. The Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) issued a new order this week 18 allowing existing Indian-flagged vessels to continue trading regardless of age, provided they meet prescribed technical and safety standards. The government has also relaxed restrictions on bringing older vessels onto the Indian register. Tankers, bulk carriers and general cargo ships over 20 years old can now be considered for registration, subject to a technical review and approval process. For containerships, gas carriers and chemical tankers, the corresponding threshold is 25 years. The latest move overturns restrictions introduced in 2023 and revised in January this year, which had imposed firm age limits on ships entering and remaining in the Indian fleet. The revised standards also extend to foreign-flagged ships operating in India’s coastal trade under the Coastal Shipping Act 2025. They do not impose a general age restriction on every foreign ship making an international port call in India. The relaxation could help owners seeking to transfer older ships to the Indian flag, including containerline MSC, whose previously announced plan to register about a dozen vessels in India had reportedly encountered difficulties under the earlier age rules.

items.title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds
items.original_title: Greece Has The Most To Lose From Delays In Shipping’s Green Transition, New Analysis Finds
items.summary: Greek shipowners hold around USD 78bn of assets exposed to the global energy transition, twice the exposure of Japan, the next most exposed ship owning nation. The risk relates to declining demand for fossil fuel cargoes which could reduce the need for vessels such as LNG carriers. It is separate but related to the risks faced by all shipowners as they manage the energy transition that will also take place within international shipping, whether driven by IMO regulation adopted this December, or postponed global regulation accompanied by a patchwork of regional regulation. The new report finds that the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is the most credible route to the single global rulebook that the shipping industry, including the Union of Greek Shipowners (UGS) has called for. Supporting the NZF, the only adoptable architecture on the table at MEPC 85, is a chance to make the second one, in how shipping’s own energy transition is regulated, predictable, lower burden, less complicated and more supportive of a mix of decarbonisation strategies and pathways.” The report, Real economy consequences for Greece from success or failure of the Net-Zero Framework, is published ahead of ISWG-GHG 23 (23 to 27 November) and MEPC 85, which opens on 30 November.

Kris Vedat, CEO of Smart Sea, warns that too many operators are prioritising new software and connectivity over the infrastructure needed to support them. There’s little point investing in sophisticated technology if the underlying systems aren’t fit for purpose.” Mr Vedat believes the industry needs to move away from short-term technology fixes towards a more co-ordinated approach that includes infrastructure assessments, standardised processes and phased implementation. Technology investments should be judged on the operational value they deliver, not simply the immediate cost savings.” The lack of consistent technical standards across shipping adds to the challenge, particularly for third-party ship managers inheriting vessels with ageing IT and operational technology. (Image: UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch) British marine accident investigators are calling for changes to superyacht safety regulations after the sinking of the luxury sailing yacht Bayesian exposed gaps in vessel stability standards, liferaft requirements and crew training that could put other large sailing yachts at risk. The recommendations, contained in the UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch’s (MAIB) final report released Thursday , follow the August 2024 disaster off Sicily that killed seven people, including British technology entrepreneur Mike Lynch and his daughter. Neither the Large Commercial Yacht Code (LY2), under which Bayesian was built, nor the subsequent Red Ensign Group Yacht Code required certain monohull sailing yachts to be assessed for the risk of being knocked onto their sides by high winds when operating without sails. It has also urged the Met Office to raise the treatment of rare but potentially catastrophic weather events with the World Meteorological Organization, while calling for updated guidance in Admiralty nautical publications. “Our investigation found that Bayesian had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised,” said Rob Loder, the UK’s Chief Inspector of Marine Accidents.

items.summary: Expeditors is rethinking its approach to acquisitions, and is already evaluating opportunities in technology, a major shift for a forwarder that has built most of its global network through organic growth. “For the last 10 years, we have been very quiet in this zone and not looking at M&A almost in any regard. That has changed,” chief financial officer Dave Hackett told the company’s first investor day in 11 years. Expeditors ranked strategic transactions second among its capital allocation priorities, behind organic investment and ahead of returning excess cash to shareholders. The prospect of M&A prompted an analyst to ask how Expeditors would integrate another business while preserving the culture its executives had spent much of the morning describing. He pointed to technology capabilities as an example of an area where Expeditors had historically been quiet, even for smaller transactions. In June, Expeditors notified Washington State of plans to cut about 230 jobs in its Global Technology division. He described the 1986 purchase of Pac Bridge, which took Expeditors into ocean freight, as probably its last major acquisition. A more recent deal shows how it has bought a specific capability: in 2020, Expeditors acquired Fleet Logistics’ digital platform to support Koho, its online less-than-truckload shipping service.

items.title: US truckers feel the squeeze as fuel price outpaces freight rates
items.original_title: US truckers feel the squeeze as fuel price outpaces freight rates
items.summary: US shippers using road haulage are increasingly abandoning annual freight contracts in favour of shorter-term agreements, as soaring diesel prices outpace freight rate increases, according to new research from EASE Logistics. The Ohio-based 3PL and 4PL provider’s Q3 26 Automotive Freight Index revealed a sharp shift in procurement strategies, with annual contracts falling from 80% of its automotive bids in September 2025 to just 45% a year later. In food and beverage, the proportion dropped from 81% to 51% by August as shippers sought “greater flexibility amid volatile transport costs”. Diesel prices exceeded $6 a gallon in September for the first time, fuel costs rising considerably faster than freight rates, which EASE reported had increased 27% year on year, compared with a 54% surge in diesel prices. Refrigerated linehaul rates, meanwhile, were up 24% at the end of August, against a 50% increase in fuel costs. Although contract pricing is beginning to catch up, with EASE’s contract cost per mile rising 6.5% between Q2 and Q3, spot rates declined 2% over the same period. Regional disparities are also emerging, particularly in the south-east, where electric vehicle-related freight lanes into Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama recorded average year-on-year rate growth of 35.6%, compared with 27.4% nationally.

items.title: Mexico-US cargo charters still facing long wait for approval
items.original_title: Mexico-US cargo charters still facing long wait for approval
items.summary: Mexican cargo airlines are still facing longer waits for US approval of cross-border charter flights, even after Washington lifted restrictions on passenger services from Mexico City to the US last month. In October 2025, the US sanctioned Mexican carriers in protest over their government’s decision in 2023 to ban freighters from Mexico City’s Benito Juarez Airport (AICM) and curtail take-off slots at the chronically congested airport, steps Washington deemed a violation of the aviation bilateral agreement between the two countries. Faced with further sanctions and a possible downgrading of its aviation security rating, the Mexican government returned slots taken from US carriers and agreed to allow freighters to return to AICM when operations were not congested. It noted that airfreight volumes of electronic components and equipment had risen by 40% this year and expressed hopes for stronger connections to key US markets like Los Angeles, Chicago, New York, and Miami. However, charters, which account for a significant portion of cross-border airfreight traffic, continue to face extended approval times, confirmed Robert Van De Weg, CEO of Mexican cargo airline mas.

items.title: Stamford firms up 10 MR tankers in China
items.original_title: Stamford firms up 10 MR tankers in China
items.summary: Singapore-based Stamford Shipping has firmed up an order for 10 MR product tankers at China’s Nantong CIMC Sinopacific Offshore & Engineering (CIMC SOE), with the yard also securing two vessels of the same design from an unidentified European owner. The shipbuilder, part of Hong Kong-listed CIMC Enric, has confirmed that construction contracts covering all 12 ships are now effective, according to a Chinese shipbuilding industry report published on November 16. Each vessel will have a capacity of 49,900 dwt, giving the combined order a total of nearly 600,000 dwt. The deal marks the yard’s entry into the MR product tanker segment, adding a new vessel type to a portfolio dominated by LNG bunkering ships, LPG and ammonia carriers, and feeder containerships. Stamford’s involvement first emerged in August, when shipbuilding sources linked the Singapore owner to 10 tankers at the Nantong yard. Stamford has been active in secondhand tankers and bulkers in recent years. The company was previously linked to the acquisition of four ultramaxes from Belships in 2025, while the newbuilding programme would represent a substantial expansion of its tanker interests. For CIMC SOE, the order extends a diversification drive that has already taken the gas carrier specialist into feeder containership construction. The yard has secured orders from owners including Danaos and Euroseas.

items.title: Last-ditch bid to prevent threatened strike at San Pedro Bay ports
items.original_title: Last-ditch bid to prevent threatened strike at San Pedro Bay ports
items.summary: A strike could disrupt cargo operations at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach from Saturday, after the latest contract negotiations between employers and port security workers ended without agreement. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents shipping lines and terminal operators, warned yesterday that a walkout was a real possibility after talks with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 broke down on Tuesday – each side blaming the other for the lack of progress. Local 26 represents approximately 250 watchmen responsible for security duties, including checking credentials at terminal entrances and conducting patrols. Although they account for only around 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, a strike could have significant consequences for cargo movements. According to the PMA, approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of LA’s is handled at the terminals where Local 26 members work. Yesterday, the PMA claimed the union had made little progress towards accepting its proposals and was unwilling to extend the current contract beyond 12:01 am on 21 November. Its offer included a one-time $3,200 bonus and wage increases that would bring average annual earnings for full-time watchmen to $198,000, alongside employer-funded healthcare and improved pension benefits.

items.summary: Star Bulk Carriers Corp., a global shipping company focusing on the transportation of dry bulk cargoes, today announced its unaudited financial and operating results for the third quarter of 2026. “Star Bulk delivered another strong quarter, with Net Income of $141.9 million, EBITDA of $192.6 million, and a TCE of $24,616 per vessel per day for the third quarter of 2026. Net cash provided by operating activities for the third quarter of 2026 was $161.0 million, compared to $91.8 million for the third quarter of 2025. Charter-in hire expenses for the third quarter of 2026 decreased to $12.8 million, compared with $15.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. Dry docking expenses for the third quarter of 2026 amounted to $17.1 million, compared to $28.1 million for the corresponding period in 2025. Vessel management fees in the third quarter of 2026 amounted to $5.6 million compared to $5.9 million for the corresponding period in 2025.

items.title: Oil prices edge higher as report says Trump considering more Iran strikes
items.original_title: Oil prices edge higher as report says Trump considering more Iran strikes
items.summary: Oil prices rose on Thursday amid caution over more Middle East supply disruptions after a report said U.S. President Donald Trump was weighing renewed military action against Iran. Crude also benefited from bargain buying after tumbling to two-month lows earlier in November, amid growing concerns over a supply glut. Brent oil futures rose 0.5% to $92.41 a barrel by 01:41 ET (06:41 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 0.1% to $83.36 a barrel. Trump considers more military strikes on Iran- NYT Gains in crude came chiefly after the New York Times reported that Trump was considering another round of extensive military strikes on Iran, amid mounting pressure from Israel. The International Energy Administration last week warned of a potential supply glut for crude, starting in the fourth quarter of 2026. The IEA said improving Middle East production and sluggish global fuel demand were likely to see supplies overshoot demand in Q4 and 2027. inventory data released on Wednesday showed a second straight week of inventory builds, adding to concerns over slowing fuel demand, especially as the winter season approaches. The greenback hit a 19-month high this week amid growing conviction that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates in December.

items.title: Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October: Monthly Intelligence Report
items.original_title: Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October: Monthly Intelligence Report
items.summary: This analysis was produced by Windward’s Maritime Intelligence Operations Center (MIOC), a mission-critical capability powered by Windward’s maritime intelligence experts and operating as a seamless extension of your team. Sanctioned Tankers Carry 60% of Russian Oil in October Sixty percent of Russian oil was shipped on sanctioned tankers throughout October, supported by a rising number of new shadow fleet entrants over 2026 that are being used to offset freight logistics inefficiencies and restrictions. Analysis of tankers calling at Russian ports to load crude, fuel oil and refined products last month found that EU-owned tankers shipped 14% of volumes, one of the lowest percentages recorded this year. Sanctioned tankers were mostly used for crude shipments (69% of barrels shipped), followed by refined products (42%) and fuel oil (30%). The overall figure of 60% carried on sanctioned tankers compares with 55% in September and 67% in March. Naval Boardings Push Sanctioned Tankers To Reflag to Russian Of the 143 sanctioned tankers tracked calling at Russian Baltic, Black Sea, Arctic and Far East ports in October, 48% (69 ships) were flagged with Russia.

items.title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.original_title: US ethanol offers lower GHG abatement costs than methanol, ammonia: study
items.summary: US corn-based ethanol could offer shipowners a cheaper route to reducing greenhouse gas emissions than low-carbon methanol and ammonia, potentially opening a new marine fuel market for American producers as the global fleet of methanol-capable vessels expands, according to a study released last week. Ethanol could abate about 2.09 metric tons of CO2 equivalent for every $1,000 spent on fuel, compared with 1.30 mt for low-carbon methanol and 1.73 mt for low-carbon ammonia, the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance, an initiative by the nonprofit Global Centre for Green Fuels, said in the study. MEMA estimated ethanol’s well-to-wake greenhouse gas intensity at 34.9 grams of CO2e/megajoule, compared with 15 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon methanol and 10 gCO2e/MJ for low-carbon ammonia. In the study, based on classification society ABS’s technical analysis, MEMA assumed US corn ethanol prices on a free-on-board Houston basis at $750/mt, equivalent to $1,125/mt of very low sulfur fuel oil on an energy-adjusted basis. The study’s indicative mid-2026 prices showed ethanol remained substantially more expensive than conventional bunkers but offered lower costs than other low-carbon alternatives. US ethanol supply The US produced 16.4 billion gallons of ethanol in 2025, against an installed capacity of 18.5 billion gallons/year, leaving about 2 billion gallons of spare capacity, according to the study.

items.title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.original_title: COSCO port fuels growth in APEC trade
items.summary: As leaders and delegates focus on advancing regional economic integration under the framework of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a transformative megaproject on the eastern Pacific coast stands as a powerful testament to these shared goals. Chancay Port in Peru, a vital APEC economy, has rapidly evolved into a pivotal logistics hub connecting Latin America with Asia, breathing life into the vision of a seamlessly interconnected Asia-Pacific. Inaugurated in November 2024, the port was hailed by Chinese President Xi Jinping as the starting point of an Inca Trail of the New Era. By slashing the one-way maritime transit time between Peru and China from roughly 35 days to just 23 days, the deep-water port has reduced logistics costs by more than 20 percent, fundamentally reshaping trans-Pacific trade dynamics. Carlos Aquino, director of the Center for Asian Studies at Peru’s National University of San Marcos, said that if Brazil routes its cargo through Chancay to China, it could save upwards of 15 days in transport time, highlighting the port’s immense geopolitical and economic magnitude. Over the past two years, the port has generated $3.65 billion in import and export trade, handling half a million twenty-foot equivalent units of containers. It is projected to bring $4.5 billion in annual economic benefits to Peru and create over 8,000 direct jobs.

items.title: Soybeans Fall as Dollar Firms
items.original_title: Soybeans Fall as Dollar Firms
items.summary: Soybean futures fell around $12.1 per bushel, easing from multi-week highs as a surging US dollar weighed on the broader grain complex. The greenback climbed to a 19-month high on growing expectations of an interest-rate hike next month, making US supplies more expensive for overseas buyers and reducing their appeal against competing origins. Higher-than-expected US soybean oil stocks also weighed on the vegetable oil market, while lower energy prices further weakened soybean oil and contributed to declines across other commodities. Meanwhile, grain markets continued to monitor the outcome of the Trump-Xi meeting, with Chinese purchases of US agricultural products remaining a key point in bilateral trade discussions. China is nearing its separate commitment to buy 25 million tonnes of US soybeans this year, but progress on a broader $17 billion farm-purchase pledge has lagged, leaving uncertainty over the outlook for US export demand. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: ALNG locks in LNG duo with oil major
items.original_title: ALNG locks in LNG duo with oil major
items.summary: Norwegian LNG carrier owner ALNG has secured period charters for both its vessels with an unnamed international oil major, taking its entire fleet out of the spot market after a difficult third quarter. The Oslo-listed company, formerly known as Awilco LNG, disclosed that it entered into contracts in October for the 2013-built, 156,000 cu m sisterships WilPride and WilForce . Both vessels have been fixed for worldwide trading, although ALNG said their final charter periods depend on certain conditions. The fixtures follow a period of weak employment for the two-vessel owner. The WilPride completed a six-month charter in early September before moving into the spot market, while the WilForce spent the third quarter trading spot with periods of inactivity. ALNG reported a third-quarter net loss of $5.9m, compared with a $6.4m loss in the preceding quarter. Fleet utilisation improved to 73% from 66%, with average time charter equivalent earnings rising to $38,400 per day from $32,600. Interim chief executive Jens-Julius Nygaard said the new agreements would improve utilisation and reduce the cost of keeping vessels idle during the winter. The move comes after ALNG embarked on a management overhaul earlier this year, including the departure of long-serving chief executive Jon Skule Storheill and a subsequent company rebranding.
